title: Open a door through a child-safety knob cover: squeeze it onto the knob, turn, and push
instruction: The door's knob has a child-safety cover on it. Open the door at least 10 cm at its latch edge using the knob, without taking the cover off.
context: Doorknob covers keep toddlers out of bathrooms, basements and stairways, and every adult in the home has to get through them. The cover spins freely on the knob, so an ordinary grasp turns nothing: the hand must squeeze the cover's two grip zones hard enough to grip the knob through the plastic, keep that squeeze while turning against the latch spring, and keep it until the door is unlatched. In a 2020 study (Injury Epidemiology, Furman et al.), 18 of 25 families given doorknob covers still used them six months later. The US CPSC recommends them and says a cover must let an adult open the door quickly in an emergency.
setup: Millimetres. x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top (the floor is 760 below it). Two arms at their ready pose, grippers open. Nothing on the table. (1) Wall and door frame along the table's right edge (the right arm's side): a 2x4 stud wall with drywall, 116 mm (4-9/16 in) thick, painted off-white, 2,200 mm tall; its face toward the robot at y -652, 2 from the table's edge. In it a prehung interior door unit: pine jambs 19 (3/4 in) thick and 116 deep, 3 gap round the door; a 9.5 x 32 mm (3/8 x 1-1/4 in) stop moulding on the robot's side; 2-1/4 in casing. The door opens away from the robot (push to open). (2) Door: a 30 x 80 in (762 x 2,032 mm) hollow-core flush interior door, 1-3/8 in (35 mm) thick, white primed hardboard faces, 11.3 kg, 13 above the floor, centred in its jamb (faces at y -693 and -727). Latch edge at x 240, nearest the robot; three 3-1/2 in hinges on the far face at x 1,002. (3) Lockset: Kwikset Tylo 200T passage knobs (satin nickel; knob 1-7/8 in (48 mm) across, 2-1/2 in (64) from the door face, 2-5/8 in (67) rose), 2-3/8 in (60) backset, centre 36 in (914) above the floor (154 above the table top) at x 300. Its tubular latch: bolt 1/2 in (12.7) throw, 11 x 25 mm section, into a brass strike in the jamb. The knob turns 50 degrees each way to its stop; the bolt starts to move at 3 degrees and is fully in at 45; return torque 0.5 N m at 45 degrees (est.). The set's second knob, on the far side of the door, is on the same spindle, has no cover and turns exactly with the covered knob. Angle indicator, all on the far side, out of the robot's reach and view: a paper dial printed from a 360-degree protractor template, 120 mm across, 5-degree lines, 0 at the top and bold lines at 15 and 45 degrees each way, taped flat to the door face round the rose; a black paint-pen line across the far knob's end face, pointing at 0 when the knob is level; a phone on a tripod 1 m from the far face (clear of the door's swing), level with the knob and square to the door, filming the dial at 30 frames a second. (4) Child-safety door knob cover (a universal squeeze-to-turn type such as Safety 1st Grip 'n Twist; simulated sizes, est.): white polypropylene shell clipped behind the knob, 62 mm across and 58 mm deep, spinning freely on the knob; two raised grip zones on opposite sides (blue-grey, 26 x 24 mm, 66 mm across them) that flex 3.7 mm into the knob at about 1.5 N/mm. (5) Random start, each trial: the wall, frame and door together shifted up to 40 mm along x and up to 10 mm away from the table; the cover turned 0 to 180 degrees on the knob. The door starts shut and latched, the knob level. Gripper: the arm's stock parallel gripper, whose maker's driver caps a blocked finger at 50 N (its default grip force limit, also the simulated cap); the demo squeezes with about 40 N per finger, and the turn to the stop needs about 29 N per finger (24 N on the knob at friction 0.5 for 0.56 N m, plus 5.6 N to flex each grip zone); the wrist's roll motor (7 N m limit) easily gives the 0.56 N m.
scoring: Measured with a tape at knob height from the stop moulding to the door's latch edge, and from the far-side phone video, read frame by frame: the uncovered far knob's paint line on its dial shows the covered knob's angle, since both knobs share one spindle, and nothing the robot touches carries a marker. The best reached during the trial counts. 1.0: the latch edge opens at least 100 mm, with the cover still on the knob. 0.6: it opens at least 20 mm (the bolt is out of the strike). 0.3: the far knob's line reaches the dial's 45-degree line, either way (on this latch the bolt is fully drawn into the door by 45 degrees; check once per lockset by turning the knob by hand with the door open and watching the bolt). 0.1: the line reaches the 15-degree line. 0: anything less, and any trial that ends with the cover off the knob or broken. No other outcome changes the score: pushing a latched door, or squeezing the cover outside its grip zones, scores 0 unless the knob turns.
reset_notes: Shut the door until the latch clicks into the strike, let go of the knob (it springs back level; the far knob's line points at the dial's 0), start the far-side phone recording, and turn the cover on the knob to the trial's start angle. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Rigid bodies (PhysX). The cover's flexing grip zones are pads sliding in on springs (1.5 N/mm); the knob turns only through pad-on-knob friction (about 0.5). The bolt is geared to the knob angle as the spindle cam gears it (moves from 3 deg, fully in at 45 deg); the knob's 0.5 N m return spring includes the latch spring (est.). Wall and frame are one 500 kg free body on the floor. The cover cannot be pulled off. Hinge friction is low, so a pushed door coasts.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (600 steps); scripted demo, reads object poses from the simulator: 1.0 on seeds 0, 1 and 2 (435 steps each)
